analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law requiring prevailing wages on federally funded construction projects.
analysis.headline: The bill to strike the Davis-Bacon wage requirement died in committee without ever reaching a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federally financed construction to pay the locally prevailing wage. This bill would wipe out that requirement, letting contractors pay whatever the market allows on federal projects. It was introduced by Representative Connie Mack with 18 Republican cosponsors, referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, and sent to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction contractors on federal projects, who could lower their labor costs by paying less than the local prevailing wage. Supporters argued taxpayers would save money through cheaper bids.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals subchapter IV of chapter 31 of title 40, U.S. Code, which contains the Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirement, effective 30 days after enactment while leaving existing contracts untouched. [S3]
The bill's stated purpose is to eliminate the wage rate requirements commonly known as the Davis-Bacon Act. [S1]

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally financed projects, who would lose the guarantee of the locally prevailing wage for their trade and could see their pay fall.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Davis-Bacon removes the wage floor for laborers and mechanics on federally financed construction, so their pay would no longer be pegged to the local prevailing rate for their trade. [S2]

The prevailing wage mandate applies to construction, alteration, and repair of public buildings and public works, so a repeal would affect a large share of government construction work, not a narrow slice. [S2]

The bill contained no transition protection for workers beyond leaving contracts already in effect or already bid out unchanged, meaning pay standards would drop for new work almost immediately after enactment. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Taxpayers might save some money on federal construction bids if contractors no longer had to pay prevailing wages, but the savings would come directly out of construction workers' paychecks. The bill offered nothing to cushion that loss for the workers affected, which is why repealing a wage floor is a straight trade of worker pay for lower public contract prices.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Connie Mack introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act on February 16, 2011, joined by 18 Republican cosponsors including Representatives Broun, Paul, Chaffetz, Flake, Jordan, and others. [S3]
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced. [S5]
On March 4, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, which is where the action history ends. [S5]
No further action, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded for the bill through the end of the 112th Congress. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers kept the prevailing wage protection on federal projects, since no vote was ever taken on repealing it.

for.name: Connie Mack
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act and recruited 18 cosponsors for it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never scheduled it for committee consideration; it went only to a subcommittee and died there.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat supported the bill. [S4]

industries.note: Without Davis-Bacon, contractors bidding on federal construction could cut labor costs by paying below the local prevailing wage, giving them an edge in bids. The gain to contractors comes directly out of construction workers' pay.

industries.industry: Building trades unions and unionized construction workers
industries.note: Union contractors survive in federal bidding partly because Davis-Bacon limits the advantage of low-wage competitors, and their members' pay is pegged to prevailing rates. Repeal would undercut both, which is why the trade is generally aligned with the workers it covers.

industries.industry: Federal and state taxpayers (government purchasers of construction)
industries.note: Government agencies fund most of the affected contracts, so cheaper bids could lower their costs. That saving is real only if it does not come entirely out of the labor share, which is what prevailing wage rules are designed to prevent.
